sections.title: Numbers up to 1000
sections.explanation: In Grade 2 we read, write and compare numbers up to 1000. Numbers help us count cricket scores, bus seats and festival sweets. We find which number comes before, after or between two numbers. We also put numbers in order from smallest to biggest, just like lining up friends by height on Sports Day.
points: Count forward and backward by 1s
Find before, after and between numbers
Compare using symbols > < =
Order numbers from smallest to biggest
Read three-digit numbers in words and numerals

sections.title: Place Value (Ones, Tens, Hundreds)
sections.explanation: Every digit sits in a special place that gives it value. Ones are single units, tens are groups of ten, and hundreds are groups of one hundred. Expanded form shows a number as a sum of these values. Shopkeepers use place value when they write prices on boards at the sabzi mandi.
points: Ones place = value of 1s
Tens place = groups of 10
Hundreds place = groups of 100
345 = 300 + 40 + 5 in expanded form
A zero can hold a place, like in 708

sections.title: Odd and Even Numbers
sections.explanation: Even numbers can be shared equally into two groups with nothing left over. Odd numbers leave one friend without a pair. Looking at the ones digit is a quick trick: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd. You can sort chalk sticks or tiffin spoons into pairs to check.
points: Even numbers end with 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8
Odd numbers end with 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9
Even numbers make equal pairs with no leftover
Odd + odd = even; even + even = even
Odd + even = odd

sections.title: Skip Counting by 2s, 5s and 10s
sections.explanation: Skip counting means jumping forward by the same number each time. Counting by 2s is like hopping on both feet. Counting by 5s matches the 5-rupee coins in your pocket. Counting by 10s is useful for bundles of notebooks or cricket overs. Skip counting also builds strong multiplication tables.
points: Skip counting helps with money and time
It links to the 2, 5 and 10 times tables

sections.title: Addition (with & without carrying)
sections.explanation: Addition finds the total when groups join together. Always line up ones under ones and tens under tens. If the ones add up to 10 or more, carry 1 ten to the tens column. Word clues like altogether, in all and total tell you to add — useful when packing festival sweets or counting children on the school bus.
points: Start adding from the ones column
Carry 1 ten when ones sum is 10 or more
Keywords: in all, altogether, total, sum
Adding zero does not change a number
Change the order: 12 + 5 = 5 + 12

sections.title: Subtraction (with & without borrowing)
sections.explanation: Subtraction finds how many are left or how much more one number is than another. Line up the places carefully. If ones are too small, borrow 1 ten and turn it into 10 ones. Words like left, remain, difference and how many more signal subtraction — think of ice cream money after a treat at the fair.
points: Keywords: left, remain, difference, how many more
Borrow when ones digit is too small
Check: difference + smaller number = bigger number
Subtracting zero leaves the number unchanged
Start from ones, then tens, then hundreds

sections.title: Multiplication & Tables
sections.explanation: Multiplication is a fast way to do repeated addition. Equal groups of idlis in tiffin boxes or rows of chairs in assembly can be written with the × sign. Learning tables from 1 to 10 (each up to ×12) makes shopping and sharing quicker. Remember: any number times 1 stays the same, and any number times 0 is 0.
points: Any number × 1 = the same number
Any number × 0 = 0
Practise tables 1–10 up to ×12
Arrays and equal groups show multiplication

sections.title: Division (Equal Sharing)
sections.explanation: Division means sharing fairly or making equal groups. If 12 sweets go to 3 friends, each friend gets the same number. You can check division with multiplication: if 12 ÷ 3 = 4, then 3 × 4 must equal 12. Never divide by zero. Sharing cricket balls into kits or laddoos into plates uses division every day.
points: Keywords: share, equally, each, groups of
Check answers by multiplying
You cannot divide by zero
Division undoes multiplication

sections.title: Word Problems & Estimation
sections.explanation: Word problems tell a short story with numbers. First read carefully and underline what is asked. Decide whether to add, subtract, multiply or divide using clue words. Estimation means finding a sensible near answer — round to the nearest ten at the market before you pay. Always write the answer with the correct unit, like rupees, children or metres.
points: Read the story twice before choosing an operation
Add for total / altogether; subtract for left / difference
Multiply for equal groups; divide for equal sharing
Write a number sentence, then solve
Label the answer with a unit
Estimate by rounding to the nearest ten

sections.title: Fractions (Half & Quarter)
sections.explanation: A fraction names an equal part of a whole. Half means the whole is cut into 2 equal parts and we take 1. Quarter means 4 equal parts and we take 1. Parts must be equal — like sharing a roti fairly at dinner. Uneven pieces are not true halves or quarters.
points: 1/2 means one half of a whole
1/4 means one quarter (one-fourth)
Fraction parts must be equal in size
Two halves make one whole
Four quarters make one whole

sections.title: 2D and 3D Shapes
sections.explanation: Flat shapes on paper are 2D shapes — they have length and breadth but no thickness. Solid objects you can hold are 3D shapes — they take up space. A window looks like a rectangle (2D), while a cricket ball is a sphere (3D). Counting sides, corners, faces and edges helps us name each shape.
points: 2D: triangle (3 sides), square, rectangle, circle
Square has 4 equal sides; rectangle has opposite sides equal
Circle has no corners
3D: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone
A dice is a cube; a football is a sphere

sections.title: Perimeter Intro (Around a Shape)
sections.explanation: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. Imagine walking along the fence of a rectangular garden or the border of a school playground. For a rectangle, add length + breadth + length + breadth, or use 2 × (length + breadth). Always use the same unit, like metres of rope.
points: Perimeter = total length of the boundary
Rectangle: add all four sides
Or use 2 × (length + breadth)
Square: 4 × side length
Units stay the same (cm or m)

sections.title: Patterns (Numbers & Shapes)
sections.explanation: A pattern follows a repeating rule you can discover. Colour patterns, shape patterns and number patterns all use a steady jump or order. Rangoli designs at Diwali and marching bands at Republic Day show patterns. Once you find the rule, you can predict what comes next.
points: Look for what repeats: colour, size or shape
Number patterns often add or subtract the same amount
Skip counting makes number patterns
Draw the next term before writing it
Check your rule works for every step

sections.title: Measurement (Length, Weight & Capacity)
sections.explanation: We measure length with centimetres and metres, weight with grams and kilograms, and liquids with millilitres and litres. Choosing a sensible unit stops silly answers — like measuring a pencil in kilometres! Time and clocks have their own special lessons next.
points: 100 cm = 1 metre
1000 g = 1 kilogram
1000 ml = 1 litre
Choose units that fit the object
Compare longer/shorter and heavier/lighter

sections.title: Reading the Clock (Hours, Minutes & Seconds)
sections.explanation: A clock helps us know when to wake up, catch the school bus, eat lunch and go to bed. Look at a round (analogue) clock: the face has numbers 1 to 12. The short hand is the hour hand — it moves slowly. The long hand is the minute hand — it moves faster. Some clocks also have a thin second hand that ticks around once every minute. Digital clocks show numbers like 8:30. We practise simple times first: o’clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to.
points: Short hand = hours; long hand = minutes; thin hand (if any) = seconds
60 seconds = 1 minute; 60 minutes = 1 hour; 24 hours = 1 day
When the long hand is on 12, we say “o’clock” (for example 3:00 is 3 o’clock)
Long hand on 6 = half past (30 minutes); on 3 = quarter past (15 minutes); on 9 = quarter to (45 minutes)
Count minutes in jumps of 5 around the clock: 5, 10, 15 … 60
Morning and afternoon: we often say a.m. (before noon) and p.m. (after noon) on a 12-hour clock

sections.title: 12-Hour and 24-Hour Time (Simple)
sections.explanation: Most home clocks are 12-hour clocks: the hands go around twice each day — once from midnight to noon, and once from noon to midnight. To tell morning from evening we use a.m. and p.m. Example: 8:00 a.m. is school time; 8:00 p.m. is bedtime story time. A 24-hour clock (often on phones, buses or railway boards) counts from 0 to 23 and does not need a.m./p.m. Afternoon and night times are bigger numbers: 15:00 means 3:00 p.m. For Grade 2 we only learn easy matches.
points: 12-hour clock uses numbers 1–12 plus a.m. (morning) or p.m. (afternoon/evening)
a.m. = after midnight until before noon; p.m. = after noon until before midnight
Noon is 12:00 in the middle of the day; midnight starts a new day
24-hour time: morning looks similar (8:00 → 08:00); afternoon adds 12 to the hour (3 p.m. → 15:00)
Easy memory: school morning ≈ a.m.; after-lunch play ≈ p.m.
Same moment can be written two ways: 4:00 p.m. = 16:00

sections.title: Calendar, Days and Months
sections.explanation: A calendar shows days, weeks and months. Knowing the date helps us plan holidays, birthdays and school tests. Seven days make one week. About four weeks make one month. Twelve months make one year. We use calendars and clocks together: the calendar says which day, the clock says what time.
points: 7 days = 1 week; 12 months = 1 year
Days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday
Months have 28, 29, 30 or 31 days
Yesterday → today → tomorrow
Festivals and birthdays are marked on calendars

sections.title: Money (Rupees & Paise)
sections.explanation: In India we use rupees (₹) and paise. One hundred paise make one rupee. At the canteen or market we add prices and subtract what we spend to find money left. We can make the same amount with different notes and coins. Counting carefully stops mistakes when buying snacks after school.
points: 100 paise = ₹1
Money left = money had − money spent
Add prices to find the total bill
Count notes and coins carefully
Same amount can be made in different ways

sections.title: Data Handling (Pictographs)
sections.explanation: Data is information we collect, like favourite fruits in class. A pictograph shows data with pictures. Always read the key — sometimes one picture means one child, sometimes it means two or five. Comparing picture rows tells you which choice is most or least popular after a monsoon picnic vote.
points: Collect and count carefully
Read the key (e.g. 1 ⭐ = 1 child)
Compare which row has more or less
Title the pictograph so others understand
One picture can stand for more than one thing
